newsitem.title: USA: Ex-employees accuse Jackson aides of harassment.
newsitem.headline: Ex-employees accuse Jackson aides of harassment.

text.p: A lawyer for five ex-employees of Michael Jackson alleged on Wednesday that they were harassed after being called to testify before a grand jury probing child molestation allegations against the star.

In opening arguments in the civil trial of a wrongful termination lawsuit, attorney Michael Ring said the five former employees at Jackson's Neverland Ranch would seek "into the millions of dollars" in damages against the so-called King of Pop and six aides.
A jury of 10 women and two men is hearing the case in Santa Barbara County Superior Court in Santa Maria, 125 miles (200 km) north of Los Angeles.

Ring accused Jackson's personal bodyguards, members of his "Office of Special Services" (OSS), of launching a campaign of harassment and intimidation against some of the former employees after they were ordered in the spring of 1994 to testify before two grand juries investigating child molestation allegations against Jackson.
"There was a concerted effort by the OSS staff to keep the plaintiffs quiet," he said.
Ring said the bodyguards made death threats against the plaintiffs and others, stared menacingly at them, made harassing telephone calls and displayed their guns in a menacing fashion.

Three of Jackson's former bodyguards, a maid and an administrative assistant sued Jackson and six of his aides, alleging they installed recording devices at his ranch to find out what they knew about molestation allegations against him. The plaintiffs say they were forced out of their jobs.
One of the ex-employees also alleges she was sexually harassed by one of Jackson's bodyguards.
Jackson denies the allegations. The pop star was not in court on Wednesday and it was not clear whether he would testify in person at the trial.
Jackson's attorney Steve Cochran said in his opening argument that, for Jackson, "this is a case about the downside of notoriety."
He accused the plaintiffs of trying to exaggerate and lie about Jackson "as part of an endeavour to shake him and the (other) defendants down in this case."
He said the allegations made by the ex-employees would be slanderous if made outside court. Their contracts allowed Jackson to fire them at any time and for any reason, he said.
Cochran will continue his opening argument when the case resumes next Tuesday after a break.
